0.title: Jesus Is Better: The Letter to the Hebrews
0.overview:
Who wrote the Letter to the Hebrews? The honest answer is: we do not know. Origen, the great third-century scholar who knew the church’s tradition better than almost anyone, concluded that only God knows who wrote it. Paul has been suggested — the theology runs as deep as any of his letters — but the literary style is far more polished and rhetorical than anything Paul wrote. Apollos, Barnabas, Priscilla, Luke — all have been proposed. In the end the mystery serves the text: Hebrews forces us to attend not to the human messenger but to the divine subject. The letter is about Jesus, and everything else in it orbits that sun.

The recipients were Jewish Christians — almost certainly a specific congregation, possibly in Rome (see 13:24, “those from Italy send you greetings”) — under intense pressure. Some had already suffered public shame, imprisonment, and the plundering of their property (10:32–34). Exhausted and frightened, they were tempted to drift back toward the synagogue, toward the familiar world of Temple sacrifice and priestly ritual. The writer’s response is not to demand more willpower but to open their eyes: you cannot go back, because going back is going backward — from substance to shadow, from fulfillment to promise, from Christ to the types that pointed toward him.

When was it written? Almost certainly before AD 70. The writer speaks of the priests and sacrifices as still going on (8:4; 10:1–3), and a letter arguing that the old system was passing away would hardly have left out the destruction of the temple if it had already happened. Timothy is alive and recently released (13:23). A date in the 60s fits best, and it matters: the readers were being drawn back to a temple that was still standing, and within a few years it would be gone.

Hebrews is structured as a “word of exhortation” (13:22) — a synagogue sermon put into written form. It alternates deliberately between doctrinal exposition and pastoral warning. The five great warning passages (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:20; 10:26–39; 12:25–29) are not interruptions to the argument; they are the argument’s pastoral urgency breaking through. Each one follows the same logic: if the lesser covenant carried consequences for violation, how much more the greater? The warnings grow in intensity as the letter progresses.

The controlling word of the letter is “better” (Greek: kreitton), used thirteen times. Jesus is the better revelation (ch. 1), the better mediator (chs. 2–3), the better rest (ch. 4), the better priest (chs. 5–7), the better covenant (ch. 8), the better sacrifice (chs. 9–10), and the ground of better and enduring possessions (ch. 10). The heroes of faith in chapter 11 were all seeking “a better country” (11:16). The letter culminates in the vision of Mount Zion, “the city of the living God” (12:22), and the unshakeable kingdom that no earthly power can topple (12:28).

Read Hebrews as a sustained pastoral argument for the all-sufficiency of Jesus Christ. Every argument leads back to him; every exhortation is grounded in him. The great High Priest has passed through the heavens, has offered himself once for all, has sat down at the right hand of God, and now — this is the astonishing thing — he continues to intercede for us. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever (13:8). Whatever the pressure, whatever the temptation to settle for something less, Hebrews speaks with one voice: hold fast to Jesus. There is nothing better. There is no one better. He is enough.

1.title: The Majesty on High: God Has Spoken His Final Word
1.overview:
Hebrews opens with no greeting, only a thunderclap. In four verses the writer sketches the Son across all of history: heir, creator, radiance of God’s glory, exact imprint of his nature, upholder of all things, purifier of sins, enthroned. Then the pivot of the whole letter: “he sat down”. Priests stood because their work was never done. Jesus sat because his is finished.

The chapter then compares the Son with angels, through whom the law was given (Acts 7:53). Seven Old Testament texts show that no angel was ever called God’s Son, worshipped by angels, addressed as God, or invited to sit at God’s right hand. Reduce Jesus to a prophet or teacher, and the rest of Hebrews collapses. This chapter will not allow it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — God Has Spoken by His Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hebrews opens without a greeting, like a sermon, which is what its author calls it (13:22). In the past God spoke through the prophets in fragments and in many different ways; now, at the climax of history, he has spoken in a Son. This Son is heir of everything and the one through whom God made the universe. He shines with God’s own glory, bears the exact imprint of his being, and sustains all things by his powerful word. Having made purification for sins, he took his seat at God’s right hand, and so ranks far above the angels, just as the name he has inherited is greater than theirs.
verseByVerse.theology:
Radiance and Imprint

God has not changed speaker; he has spoken finally, in a Son. Verse 3 holds together what the church later had to defend: the Son is one with the Father in nature and distinct from him in person — and, having made purification for sins, he sat down.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish Christians under pressure were thinking of going back to what was partial.

Now: The way out of an old attachment is not to call it worthless but to see what it was pointing at.

verseByVerse.quote: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,

Meaning first. Hebrews 1 opens the letter with a magnificent statement of who Jesus is. God, who spoke in many partial ways through the prophets, has now spoken his final word in his Son (vv. 1–2). The Son is described in seven great claims: heir of all things, agent of creation, radiance of God’s glory, exact imprint of his being, sustainer of the universe, the one who made purification for sins, and the one now seated at God’s right hand (vv. 2–3). He is therefore far greater than the angels (v. 4). The rest of the chapter proves this from seven Old Testament quotations (vv. 5–14): God calls the Son his Son, as he never called an angel; the angels are commanded to worship him; angels are servants, like wind and fire, but the Son is addressed as God, with an eternal throne; he is the Lord who made the earth and heavens and will outlast them; and he alone is invited to sit at God’s right hand, while the angels are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. The chapter sets the theme of the whole letter: Jesus is better, and so to turn from him would be to turn from God’s final word.

Setting and background. The author of Hebrews is not named; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, Luke, Priscilla and others have been suggested. The early church was divided: the Eastern church generally attributed it to Paul, while the Western church long doubted it. Origen, in the third century, famously said that only God knows who wrote it. The style and vocabulary are unlike Paul’s, and the author says he received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), which Paul insisted he did not (Galatians 1:12). Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian Jew mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24), fits the style well. Whoever the author was, he was a close associate of Timothy (13:23), and the church received the letter as Scripture. The readers were Jewish Christians, probably in or near Rome (13:24), written before the destruction of the temple in AD 70, since the sacrifices are spoken of as still continuing (8:4; 10:1–2). They had suffered persecution (10:32–34), were tempted to drift back to Judaism to avoid further suffering, and had grown spiritually sluggish (5:11–14). The author writes a “word of exhortation” (13:22), really a sermon, showing that Christ is better than angels, Moses, Joshua, Aaron, the old covenant and its sacrifices, and calling them to hold fast.

Long ago. Key words. “Long ago” (palai, in the past, of old). The period of the Old Testament revelation, stretching over a thousand years.

At many times and in many ways. Key words. Two alliterative words in Greek: polymerōs (in many parts, portions, fragments) and polytropōs (in many manners, modes). God spoke in many separate episodes, each giving part of the truth, and through many means: visions, dreams, voices, events, laws, symbols, poetry, prophetic actions. The revelation was real, true and from God, but partial and progressive.

God spoke to our fathers. Key words. “Spoke” (lalēsas). The God of the Bible is a speaking God (Isaiah 55:11). “Our fathers”: the ancestors of Israel. The author and readers were Jewish; the Old Testament was their heritage.

By the prophets. Key words. “By” (en, in, through). The prophets were God’s mouthpieces, including Moses, David and all the Old Testament writers (2 Peter 1:21). What they said, God said.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament revelation was false or merely human. It was God’s word, true and authoritative. The contrast is not between false and true but between partial and complete, preparation and fulfilment.

In a sentence. In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets, a little at a time and in many different ways,

For worship. Thank God that he is a God who speaks, and that he has not left us in the dark. Read the Old Testament as God’s true word, pointing to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The author of Hebrews is not named; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and others have been suggested. It was written to Jewish Christians tempted to turn back from Christ, probably before the temple fell in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.

But in these last days. Key words. “Last days” (ep’ eschatou tōn hēmerōn toutōn, at the end of these days). The prophets spoke of “the last days” as the time of the Messiah (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). With Christ’s coming, the last days have begun. We live in them now (Acts 2:17; 1 Corinthians 10:11).

He has spoken to us by his Son. Key words. Literally “in Son” (en huiō), without the article. The emphasis is on the kind of messenger: not a prophet, but one who is Son. The Son is not just another messenger in a line; he is the final, complete word (John 1:1, 18). Revelation reaches its climax in him. There is no further word to come that will surpass or add to him. This is the basis of the closed canon: the apostolic writings record and explain this final word.

Whom he appointed the heir of all things. Key words. “Heir” (klēronomon). In the ancient world, the firstborn son inherited his father’s estate. The Son is heir of everything that exists (Psalm 2:8; Matthew 28:18). Everything was made for him (Colossians 1:16), and will be summed up in him (Ephesians 1:10).

Through whom also he created the world. Key words. “World” (tous aiōnas, the ages): the universe in its entirety, space and time. The Son was the agent of creation (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 8:6). He is not a created being; he existed before creation and made it. The one who is heir at the end was the Creator at the beginning.

Where Christians differ: is revelation still ongoing? Some charismatic teaching expects ongoing prophetic revelation from God alongside Scripture; some liberal theology sees revelation as continuing through human experience. Verdict: God’s speaking in the Son is final. The apostles and their associates recorded and explained this revelation in the New Testament, and with them the canon closed (Jude 3; Revelation 22:18–19). God still illumines his word by his Spirit, applies it to our hearts, and guides us providentially, but he does not give new revelation equal to Scripture. Scripture alone is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

What it does not mean. “Appointed heir” does not mean the Son was not always divine or that he earned his status. As eternal Son, he has always been Lord; as incarnate Son, having completed his work, he was appointed heir as the God-man.

In a sentence. but in these final days he has spoken to us through one who is his Son, whom he has made heir of everything and through whom he made the universe.

For worship. Listen to the Son. Everything God has to say to you, he has said in Jesus. Read a Gospel passage today as God speaking to you.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,

He is the radiance of the glory of God. Key words. “He is” (ōn, being): present tense, his eternal state. “Radiance” (apaugasma, effulgence, brightness shining out). Either the radiance itself (as light streams from the sun) or a reflection (as a mirror reflects). Most likely the first: the Son is the outshining of God’s glory, not a separate light reflecting it. As the sun’s rays are never separate from the sun and have existed as long as the sun, so the Son is eternally one with the Father. “Glory” (doxa): the visible splendour of God’s being (Exodus 33:18–23; John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 4:6).

And the exact imprint of his nature. Key words. “Exact imprint” (charaktēr, the impression made by a seal or die, an exact representation; our word “character”). “Nature” (hypostaseōs, essence, substance, being). As a seal leaves its exact image in wax, so the Son is the exact representation of the Father’s being. To see him is to see the Father (John 14:9; Colossians 1:15). Later, the church used hypostasis to mean “person,” but here it means “essence” or “being.”

And he upholds the universe by the word of his power. Key words. “Upholds” (pherōn, carries, bears along, sustains). Present tense: continuously. Not like Atlas holding up the world, but carrying it forward toward its goal. “The word of his power”: his powerful word. The same word that created sustains (Colossians 1:17). If he stopped speaking, the universe would cease. Every atom exists at his word.

After making purification for sins. Key words. “Making purification” (katharismon poiēsamenos, having made cleansing). Aorist: a completed act. The Creator and Sustainer became the priest who cleanses sin. In the Old Testament, purification was made by blood (Leviticus 16:30). Christ made purification by his own blood, once for all (9:12–14, 26). This anticipates the main theme of the letter.

He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. Key words. “Sat down” (ekathisen). Priests in the tabernacle never sat; there were no chairs, because their work was never finished (10:11). Christ sat down because his work of purification was complete (10:12). “Right hand”: the place of honour, authority and power (Psalm 110:1). “The Majesty on high”: a reverent Jewish way of referring to God.

What it does not mean. “Radiance” and “imprint” do not mean the Son is a lesser copy or a separate god. He is of the same essence as the Father, fully God, yet a distinct person (John 1:1). Nor does “sat down” mean Christ is inactive; he reigns and intercedes (7:25). It means his atoning work is finished.

In a sentence. The Son is the shining out of God’s glory and the exact expression of his being, and he keeps the whole universe going by his powerful word. After he had made cleansing for sins, he took his seat at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven,

For worship. Worship Christ as Creator, Sustainer and Saviour. The one who holds the universe together also cleansed your sins and sat down: it is finished.

verseByVerse.quote: having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.

Having become as much superior to angels. Key words. “Become” (genomenos). As the eternal Son he was always superior to angels. But in his incarnation he was made for a little while lower than the angels (2:9); by his death, resurrection and ascension, as the God-man, he was exalted far above them (Ephesians 1:20–21; Philippians 2:9). “Superior” (kreittōn, better), a keyword of Hebrews, used thirteen times: better hope, better covenant, better promises, better sacrifices, better possession, better country, better resurrection.

As the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. Key words. “Name”: in Scripture, a name expresses character, status and identity. “Inherited” (keklēronomēken, perfect tense: inherited and still holds). The name is “Son” (vv. 2, 5), which no angel bears in this unique sense. It may also include “Lord,” the name above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). “More excellent” (diaphorōteron, different, superior).

Setting and background. Why compare Christ to angels? In Jewish thought, angels were highly honoured. They were believed to have mediated the giving of the law at Sinai (2:2; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). Some Jews speculated about angels as great powers, and some may have seen Jesus as an angelic being. By showing that Christ is far superior to the angels who brought the old covenant, the author shows that the new covenant he brings is far superior too.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was once an angel, or a created being of a higher order. He created them (v. 2; Colossians 1:16). Nor does “became” mean he was not always divine. It refers to his exaltation as the incarnate Mediator.

In a sentence. and so he has become as much greater than the angels as the name he has inherited is greater than theirs.

For worship. Honour the name of Jesus above every other name, above every power seen and unseen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Seven Texts, and Not One of Them About an Angel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer proves his point entirely from Scripture. No angel was told, “You are my Son.” The angels are told to worship the Son. Angels are made winds and flames; the Son is addressed, “Your throne, O God, is forever.” Of the Son it is said, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth… you remain.” No angel was told, “Sit at my right hand.” Angels are servants sent to help those who will inherit salvation.
verseByVerse.theology:
Texts About God, Applied to Jesus

Scriptures addressed to God — Psalm 45 and Psalm 102 — are read as addressed to the Son, and the angels are commanded to worship him. A being the angels worship cannot be one of them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers who had lost property and standing were told that earth and sky are the temporary things; the Son remains.

Now: The angels, far from rivals, are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”

For to which of the angels did God ever say. Key words. A rhetorical question expecting the answer: none. Angels are sometimes called “sons of God” collectively (Job 1:6; 38:7), but God never addressed any individual angel as “my Son” in this unique sense.

You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Key words. From Psalm 2:7, a royal psalm in which God installs his King on Zion. “Today I have begotten you”: originally referring to the day of the king’s coronation, when he was declared God’s son. The New Testament applies it to Christ’s resurrection and exaltation, when he was publicly declared the Son of God in power (Acts 13:33; Romans 1:4). It does not mean he began to exist then, but that his eternal sonship was openly proclaimed and he was enthroned as the Messianic King.

I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. Key words. From God’s promise to David about his descendant (2 Samuel 7:14; 1 Chronicles 17:13). It applied first to Solomon, but ultimately to the greater Son of David, the Messiah, whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:13, 16).

And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world. Key words. “Firstborn” (prōtotokon): not first created, but pre-eminent in rank and heir (Psalm 89:27; Colossians 1:15, 18). “Brings into the world” may refer to his incarnation (Luke 2:13–14, when angels praised at his birth), his resurrection, or most likely his return in glory (“again” may go with “brings”: when he again brings the firstborn into the world).

Let all God’s angels worship him. Key words. The words of verse 6 match the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 32:43, which is longer than the Hebrew; a similar thought appears in Psalm 97:7. Angels are commanded to worship the Son. Since only God may be worshipped (Matthew 4:10; Revelation 22:8–9), this proves the Son is God.

Textual note. The Dead Sea Scrolls contain a Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 32:43 that includes the line about the gods (or angels) bowing down, which supports the Greek translation used here as reflecting an ancient Hebrew form of the text.

What it does not mean. “Today I have begotten you” does not mean the Son was created or had a beginning. The church confesses him as “eternally begotten of the Father,” a relationship without beginning. Nor does “firstborn” mean first created (as Jehovah’s Witnesses argue); it denotes supremacy and inheritance.

In a sentence. God never said to any angel, “You are my Son; today I have become your Father.” Nor did he say of any angel, “I will be his Father, and he will be my Son.” And when he brings his firstborn into the world, he says, “All God’s angels must worship him.”

For worship. Join the angels in worshipping the Son. If the highest beings in heaven bow before him, so should we.
verseByVerse.note: The words of v. 6 match the Greek Old Testament of Deut 32:43, which is longer than the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.” But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.” But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

Of the angels he says, He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire. Key words. From Psalm 104:4, following the Greek translation. “Angels” (angelous, messengers) and “winds” (pneumata, also spirits). “Ministers” (leitourgous, servants, those who perform public service). Angels are powerful, like wind and fire, but they are servants, made and used by God as he wills. Their form and function are changeable at his command.

But of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. Key words. From Psalm 45:6–7, a royal wedding psalm. The king is addressed as “O God” (ho theos, vocative). In its original setting this was striking hyperbole for a human king; its full meaning is realised only in the Messiah, who is truly God. One of the clearest statements of the Son’s deity in Scripture. Forever and ever: his kingdom is eternal (2 Samuel 7:16; Daniel 7:14; Luke 1:33). Contrast the changeable angels.

The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. Key words. “Scepter” (rhabdos, rod, staff of rule). “Uprightness” (euthytētos, straightness, justice). His rule is perfectly just (Isaiah 11:3–5).

You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Key words. Christ’s perfect moral character: he loved what is right and hated evil, perfectly, throughout his earthly life (4:15; 7:26).

Therefore God, your God, has anointed you. Key words. “God, your God”: the Son, who is addressed as God, also has God as his God. This reflects the distinction of persons in the Trinity and the Son’s role as incarnate Mediator (John 20:17). “Anointed” (echrisen), the root of “Christ” (Messiah, Anointed One). Kings and priests were anointed with oil; Christ is the anointed King.

With the oil of gladness beyond your companions. Key words. “Oil of gladness”: oil used at festivals and coronations, symbolising joy. Christ’s exaltation brings him supreme joy (12:2). “Companions” (metochous, partners, sharers): perhaps other kings, or angels, or his people who share in his kingdom (3:1, 14, where the same word appears). He is exalted above all.

What it does not mean. “God, your God” does not mean the Son is less than God. He is God the Son; in his mediatorial role as the God-man, he relates to the Father as his God. Nor does Psalm 104 deny the reality of angels; it describes their servant role.

In a sentence. About the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his servants flames of fire.” But to the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, lasts for ever and ever; your royal sceptre is a sceptre of justice. You have loved what is right and hated wrongdoing; that is why God, your God, has set you above your companions by anointing you with the oil of joy.”

For worship. Worship Christ as God, the righteous King whose throne lasts forever. Bring your life under his just sceptre today.

verseByVerse.quote: And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”

And, You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning. Key words. From Psalm 102:25–27. In the psalm, these words are addressed to Yahweh, the LORD God of Israel. The author applies them directly to the Son. What is said of Yahweh is said of Christ: he is the LORD, the Creator. “In the beginning”: echoing Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1.

And the heavens are the work of your hands. Key words. The Son made everything (v. 2).

They will perish, but you remain. Key words. “Perish” (apolountai). The present creation is not eternal. “Remain” (diameneis, continue, endure throughout). The Son is eternal.

They will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up. Key words. “Wear out” (palaiōthēsontai, grow old). Creation is like clothing that ages and frays. “Roll them up” (helixeis, fold up, like a cloak). The Son will fold up the old creation as easily as a person rolls up an old coat (Isaiah 34:4; Revelation 6:14).

Like a garment they will be changed. Key words. “Changed” (allagēsontai). Not annihilated but transformed: the old creation will be replaced by new heavens and a new earth (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1; Romans 8:19–21).

But you are the same, and your years will have no end. Key words. “The same” (ho autos): unchanging, immutable. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (13:8). “Your years will have no end”: eternal, without beginning or end. In a world of decay and change, Christ is the one unchanging reality.

What it does not mean. It does not mean creation is worthless because it will pass away. It is God’s good work, and it will be renewed. Nor does the Son’s unchangeableness mean he did not truly become human; he took on human nature without ceasing to be God.

In a sentence. And he also says, “In the beginning, Lord, you laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are what your hands have made. They will pass away, but you will remain; they will all grow old like clothing. You will roll them up like a cloak, and like clothing they will be replaced. But you stay the same, and your years will never come to an end.”

For worship. When everything around you is changing or falling apart, rest in Christ, who never changes.

verseByVerse.quote: And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?

And to which of the angels has he ever said. Key words. The final quotation returns to the question of verse 5, framing the whole series.

Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. Key words. From Psalm 110:1. Psalm 110 is the Old Testament passage most often quoted in the New Testament (Matthew 22:44; Acts 2:34–35; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Hebrews 10:12–13). Jesus himself used it to show the Messiah is David’s Lord, not merely his son (Mark 12:35–37). “Sit at my right hand”: the place of royal authority. “Until I make your enemies a footstool”: ancient kings placed their feet on the necks of conquered enemies (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns now, and his enemies are being subdued, the last enemy being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). Hebrews will later develop the priestly side of Psalm 110 (v. 4, Melchizedek).

Are they not all ministering spirits. Key words. “Ministering” (leitourgika, serving, performing service). “Spirits” (pneumata). All angels, even the highest, are servants.

Sent out to serve. Key words. “Sent out” (apostellomena, being sent, present tense: continually). “To serve” (eis diakonian, for service, ministry). Angels are God’s messengers and servants.

For the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. Key words. “Inherit” (klēronomein). The heirs of salvation are believers. Angels serve them: protecting, guiding, ministering, as Scripture shows many times (Psalm 34:7; 91:11; Acts 12:7–10; Matthew 18:10). Remarkable: the beings the readers were tempted to honour above Christ actually serve Christ’s people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should pray to angels or seek contact with them (Colossians 2:18). They serve at God’s command, not ours. Nor does it give a basis for the idea of each person having a personal guardian angel assigned for life, though angels certainly do watch over God’s people.

In a sentence. And to which of the angels did God ever say, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a stool for your feet”? Are not all the angels spirits who serve, sent out to help those who will inherit salvation?

For worship. Thank God for the unseen ministry of angels, and above all for the Son who reigns at his right hand until every enemy is defeated.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110 is the Old Testament passage most often quoted in the New.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,<sup>2</sup>but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.<sup>3</sup>He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,<sup>4</sup>having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.<sup>5</sup>For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”?<sup>6</sup>And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”<sup>7</sup>Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.”<sup>8</sup>But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.<sup>9</sup>You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”<sup>10</sup>And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands;<sup>11</sup>they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment,<sup>12</sup>like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”<sup>13</sup>And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”?<sup>14</sup>Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?

2.title: Lower Than the Angels: The Glory of the Humiliated Son
2.overview:
If chapter 1 is a summit, chapter 2 is a deliberate descent, and just as glorious. The obvious objection is: if Jesus is this exalted Son, why did he suffer and die? The answer comes through Psalm 8. Man was made to rule creation, but we do not yet see it. What we see is Jesus, made lower than the angels, tasting death for everyone, and crowned with glory. The humiliation was the road by which the founder of salvation brings many sons to glory. He shared our flesh to destroy the devil’s power and free us from the fear of death.

The chapter also contains the first of five warning passages (vv. 1–4): if the law given through angels carried penalties, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first of the letter’s warnings follows. Because of who the Son is, the readers must hold on all the more carefully to the message they heard, or they will drift away from it like a boat slipping its mooring. If the law delivered through angels was binding, and every breach of it was justly punished, there will be no escape for those who shrug off a salvation this great. It was first announced by the Lord himself, confirmed to us by those who heard him, and backed by God with signs, wonders, miracles and gifts of the Spirit given as he chose.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Danger Is Drift

The peril is not dramatic renunciation but neglect — slipping past the harbour without ever deciding to leave. The remedy is attention to what has been heard.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If the law given through angels carried penalties, neglecting the salvation declared by the Lord is more serious still.

Now: The question is not whether you have renounced Christ but whether you are still paying attention.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it. For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it. For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,

Meaning first. Hebrews 2 has two movements. First, the first of the letter’s five warnings (vv. 1–4): since the Son is so much greater than angels, his message is so much more serious than the law given through angels. If disobeying that law brought just punishment, there is no escape for those who neglect the great salvation announced by the Lord, confirmed by eyewitnesses, and attested by God with miracles and gifts of the Spirit. Second, why the Son became lower than the angels (vv. 5–18). Psalm 8 says God made humanity lower than the angels and crowned it with glory, putting everything under its feet. We do not yet see everything subject to humanity; but we do see Jesus, made lower than angels for a little while, now crowned with glory because he suffered death for others (vv. 5–9). It was fitting for God to make the pioneer of salvation perfect through suffering, so that he could bring many sons to glory; Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers (vv. 10–13). He shared our flesh and blood so that by his death he could destroy the devil, who held the power of death, and free those enslaved by fear of death (vv. 14–15). He helps the descendants of Abraham, not angels, and so he had to become like his brothers in every way, to be a merciful and faithful high priest who makes propitiation for the people’s sins and helps them when they are tempted, having been tempted himself (vv. 16–18).

Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard. Key words. “Therefore” (dia touto, because of this): because the Son is so much greater (chapter 1). “Pay much closer attention” (perissoterōs prosechein, give exceedingly greater heed). “We”: the author includes himself. “What we have heard”: the gospel.

Lest we drift away from it. Key words. “Drift away” (pararyōmen, flow past, slip away, as a ship drifts past its harbour or a ring slips off a finger). The danger is not dramatic rebellion but slow, careless drift. Neglect is enough to be lost. Nobody has to do anything to drift; they just have to stop paying attention.

For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable. Key words. Jewish tradition held that the law was given through angels (Acts 7:38, 53; Galatians 3:19; Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek translation). “Reliable” (bebaios, firm, valid, legally binding). The law was God’s binding word.

And every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution. Key words. “Transgression” (parabasis, stepping over the line, active sin). “Disobedience” (parakoē, refusing to hear, passive neglect). Both were punished. “Just retribution” (endikon misthapodosian, fair payment, deserved penalty). The law’s penalties were real and fair (Numbers 15:30–31; Deuteronomy 17:2–7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law was less from God because angels were involved. It came from God through angelic mediation. The point is the argument from lesser to greater: if the lesser message was binding, how much more the greater.

In a sentence. That is why we must pay much more careful attention to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. For if the message delivered through angels was binding, and every wrongdoing and disobedience was justly punished,

On a Tuesday. Are you drifting? Drift happens through neglect. Take a deliberate step today: read, pray, worship, gather with God’s people.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that the law was given through angels.

verseByVerse.quote: how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.

How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? Key words. “Escape” (ekpheuxometha, flee out of, get away from) the judgement. “Neglect” (amelēsantes, be careless about, disregard, not care for). The word used in Jesus’ parable of those who “paid no attention” to the wedding invitation (Matthew 22:5). Not outright rejection, but indifference. “Such a great salvation” (tēlikautēs sōtērias, so vast a salvation). The greater the gift, the greater the guilt of neglecting it.

It was declared at first by the Lord. Key words. “Declared” (laleisthai, spoken). The gospel was first spoken by the Lord Jesus himself (Mark 1:14–15). Not by angels, but by the Son.

And it was attested to us by those who heard. Key words. “Attested” (ebebaiōthē, confirmed, guaranteed, the same root as “reliable” in v. 2). Eyewitnesses, the apostles, confirmed it. The writer did not hear Jesus himself; he received the gospel from those who did. This is one reason most think Paul did not write Hebrews, since Paul insisted he received the gospel directly from Christ (Galatians 1:11–12).

While God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles. Key words. “Bore witness” (synepimartyrountos, testified together with, added his testimony). “Signs” (sēmeiois, miracles pointing to a meaning). “Wonders” (terasin, miracles that astonish). “Miracles” (dynamesin, works of power). The three words describe the miracles of Jesus and the apostles (Acts 2:22, 43; 2 Corinthians 12:12). God himself confirmed the message with supernatural evidence.

And by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will. Key words. “Gifts” (merismois, distributions, apportionings). “According to his will”: God decides who receives what gift (1 Corinthians 12:11). Notice that the signs are described in the past tense, as confirming the message “to us” in the apostolic generation.

Where Christians differ: do miraculous sign gifts continue today? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe the miraculous gifts, such as healing, tongues and prophecy, continue in the same way throughout the church age. Verdict: This verse describes the signs, wonders and miracles as God’s confirmation of the gospel through those who heard the Lord, that is, the apostolic generation (2 Corinthians 12:12). Their purpose was to authenticate the foundational revelation. With that revelation complete, the sign gifts have ceased in that form. God still works powerfully, answers prayer, heals as he wills, and gives every believer gifts for service (Romans 12:6–8; 1 Peter 4:10–11). This cessationist view is held charitably toward brothers who differ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God can no longer do miracles. He is sovereign and may act extraordinarily at any time. It means the apostolic sign gifts, given to confirm new revelation, are not a normal ongoing feature of the church.

In a sentence. how can we possibly escape if we disregard so great a salvation? It was first announced by the Lord himself, and it was confirmed to us by those who heard him, while God added his own testimony through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit given out as he chose.

On a Tuesday. Have you grown careless about the gospel? Spend time today thinking about how great your salvation is.
verseByVerse.note: The writer did not hear Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Founder Made Perfect Through Suffering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Psalm 8 says God crowned man with glory and put everything under him, but we do not yet see that. We see Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while, crowned because he suffered death for everyone. It was fitting that God should make the founder of salvation perfect through suffering, bringing many sons to glory. He is not ashamed to call them brothers. He shared flesh and blood to destroy the devil and free those enslaved by the fear of death. He was made like us in every way, to be a merciful and faithful high priest, and because he suffered when tempted, he can help those who are tempted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear of Death as Lifelong Slavery

We do not yet see everything subject to man, but we see Jesus — lowered, crowned, tasting death for everyone. He shared flesh and blood to break the devil's hold through the fear of death, and to make propitiation as a merciful and faithful high priest.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation that had lost property wondered why following a crowned Lord meant shame. The pattern he walked runs down first.

Now: Because he suffered when tempted, he is able to help those being tempted — today.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking. It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking. It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.

For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come. Key words. “Subjected” (hypetaxen, placed under authority). “The world to come” (tēn oikoumenēn tēn mellousan, the coming inhabited world): the new creation, the age inaugurated by Christ and consummated at his return. Some Jewish thought held that angels governed the nations in this age (Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Greek; Daniel 10:13, 20). But the coming world will be ruled not by angels but by Christ and his people.

It has been testified somewhere. Key words. “Somewhere” (pou): not ignorance of the reference, but a way of emphasising that what matters is what God said, not where (4:4).

What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? Key words. From Psalm 8:4–6, following the Greek translation. In the psalm, David marvels that God, who made the vast heavens, cares for tiny humanity. “Son of man” in the psalm means a human being. But the phrase also became Jesus’ favourite title for himself (Daniel 7:13), and the author sees the psalm fulfilled in Jesus as the true representative man.

You made him for a little while lower than the angels. Key words. “For a little while” (brachy ti, a little lower, or for a short time). In the Hebrew psalm, humanity is made “a little lower than God” (or “than the heavenly beings”); the Greek translation has “angels.” Humanity occupies a place in creation below the angels in power, yet crowned with dignity.

You have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet. Key words. Humanity was created to rule over creation as God’s image-bearers (Genesis 1:26–28). That was the original design.

Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. Key words. The psalm’s “everything” means everything: no exceptions.

At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. Key words. “Not yet” (oupō). The obvious problem: humanity does not rule creation as it was meant to. Sin, death, disease, disasters and the devil defy human rule. The fall disrupted God’s design (Romans 8:20–22). The psalm seems unfulfilled. The next verse gives the answer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the psalm was wrong or has failed. It awaits fulfilment, and that fulfilment has begun in Jesus. Nor does it deny that angels serve God in governing the world now; it means the age to come belongs to Christ and his redeemed people.

In a sentence. For God did not place the coming world, which we are talking about, under the authority of angels. Someone has testified somewhere: “What is a human being, that you remember him, a mortal, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour and put everything under his feet.” In putting everything under him, God left nothing that is not under him. Yet at present we do not see everything under human control.

For worship. Marvel today that the God of the universe cares for you. And thank him that what humanity lost, Christ will restore.

verseByVerse.quote: But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.

But we see him. Key words. “But” answers the problem of verse 8. We do not see humanity ruling everything; but we do see Jesus. “See” (blepomen, look at, perceive): with the eyes of faith.

Who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus. Key words. The name “Jesus” is held back until the end of the phrase for emphasis. His human name: the incarnate Son. In becoming man, he took the place of humanity, lower than the angels (Philippians 2:7–8). He is the true man, the last Adam, in whom Psalm 8 is fulfilled (1 Corinthians 15:27, 45).

Crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death. Key words. “Crowned” (estephanōmenon, perfect tense: crowned and still crowned). The psalm’s words are fulfilled in Jesus. “Because of the suffering of death”: his exaltation was the reward of his humiliation (Philippians 2:8–9). Through death to glory.

So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. Key words. “By the grace of God” (chariti theou). His death was the gift of God’s grace. “Taste death” (geusētai thanatou): experience death fully, not merely sip it (Mark 9:1). “For everyone” (hyper pantos, on behalf of each). In the context, the “everyone” are the “many sons” being brought to glory (v. 10), his “brothers” (v. 11), “the children God has given me” (v. 13), “the offspring of Abraham” (v. 16), “the people” (v. 17).

Textual note. A few manuscripts and some early church writers read “apart from God” (chōris theou) instead of “by the grace of God” (chariti theou). The two look similar in Greek. “Apart from God” might refer to Jesus’ cry of abandonment on the cross, or to his dying for all apart from God himself. But the great majority of manuscripts read “by the grace of God,” and that is almost certainly original.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every individual equally? Many read “for everyone” as proof that Christ’s death was equally for every human being, making salvation possible for all. Verdict: The surrounding verses define the “everyone” as the many sons brought to glory, the brothers he sanctifies, the children given to him by the Father (vv. 10–13). His death actually achieves their salvation: it brings them to glory, destroys the devil’s power over them, frees them, and makes propitiation for their sins (vv. 10, 14–17). This is definite atonement: Christ tasted death for each one of those he came to save, and none of them will be lost. Yet his death is of infinite value, sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to every person.

What it does not mean. “For everyone” does not mean all will be saved. Hebrews warns repeatedly that those who reject Christ face judgement (2:3; 10:26–31).

In a sentence. What we do see is Jesus, who for a short time was made lower than the angels and who is now crowned with glory and honour because he suffered death, so that by God’s grace he might experience death on behalf of each one of his people.

For worship. Look to Jesus, crowned with glory. Thank him that he tasted death for you, so that you will never taste its bitterness as judgement.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.

For it was fitting that he. Key words. “Fitting” (eprepen, appropriate, suitable, worthy of). The cross was not an embarrassing necessity but entirely fitting with God’s character and wisdom. “He” is God the Father.

For whom and by whom all things exist. Key words. “For whom” (di’ hon, for the sake of whom): God is the goal of all things. “By whom” (di’ hou, through whom): God is the cause of all things (Romans 11:36). The Creator and goal of everything chose this way of salvation.

In bringing many sons to glory. Key words. “Bringing” (agagonta, leading). “Many sons” (pollous huious): the redeemed, adopted as God’s children (Romans 8:14–17, 29). “Glory”: final salvation, sharing in Christ’s glory (Romans 8:18, 30). God’s purpose is to lead a great family home to glory.

Should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering. Key words. “Founder” (archēgon, pioneer, leader, trailblazer, originator, champion). One who goes first and opens the way for others to follow, like a pioneer cutting a path, or a champion fighting on behalf of his people (12:2; Acts 3:15; 5:31). “Perfect” (teleiōsai, complete, bring to the goal, fully qualify). A keyword of Hebrews. It does not mean Jesus was morally imperfect and needed improving; he was always sinless (4:15; 7:26). It means he was made fully qualified as Saviour and High Priest by going through suffering, testing and death. His experience of suffering completed his preparation for his office (5:8–9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus was ever sinful or deficient in character. Nor does it mean God enjoyed his Son’s suffering. It means the path to glory for the Saviour, and for his people, passes through suffering, and that this was wise and right.

In a sentence. It was right for God, for whom and through whom everything exists, in bringing many children to glory, to make the pioneer of their salvation fully qualified through suffering.

For worship. Thank Jesus, the pioneer of your salvation, who walked through suffering before you and is leading you home to glory.

verseByVerse.quote: For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.” And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.” And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”

For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified. Key words. “Sanctifies” (hagiazōn, makes holy, sets apart for God). Jesus is the one who makes his people holy, by his blood (10:10, 14; 13:12). “Those who are sanctified”: believers, set apart for God.

All have one source. Key words. Literally “are all of one” (ex henos pantes). “One” may be God (the one Father of both Jesus and believers), or Adam (shared human nature), or simply one family. Most likely God the Father: Jesus and his people share one Father and one family, and Jesus shares their humanity.

That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers. Key words. “Not ashamed” (ouk epaischynetai). Despite their sin and weakness, the exalted Son is not embarrassed to own them as his family (Matthew 12:49–50; John 20:17).

I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise. Key words. From Psalm 22:22, the psalm Jesus quoted on the cross (Psalm 22:1). The psalm moves from agony to triumph. After his suffering, the Messiah praises God among his brothers in the assembly. “Congregation” (ekklēsias, church). The risen Christ leads his church in worship.

I will put my trust in him. Key words. From Isaiah 8:17 (also 2 Samuel 22:3; Isaiah 12:2). Jesus, as a true man, lived by faith in his Father, as his brothers must. He is the supreme example of trust (12:2).

Behold, I and the children God has given me. Key words. From Isaiah 8:18. Isaiah and his children were signs to Israel. Applied to Christ: he stands with the children the Father has given him (John 6:37, 39; 10:29; 17:6). They are a gift from the Father to the Son, and he will lose none of them.

What it does not mean. “One source” does not mean believers are divine as Jesus is. He is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. He is the Sanctifier; we are the sanctified.

In a sentence. The one who makes people holy and those who are made holy belong to the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters. He says, “I will declare your name to my brothers and sisters; in the assembly I will sing your praises.” And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Here I am, and the children God has given me.”

For worship. Jesus is not ashamed of you. Let that move you to worship him, and to not be ashamed of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.

Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood. Key words. “Share” (kekoinōnēken, have in common, perfect tense: a settled condition). “Flesh and blood” (haimatos kai sarkos): human nature, with its weakness and mortality.

He himself likewise partook of the same things. Key words. “Partook” (meteschen, took a share in, aorist: a definite moment). The incarnation. The eternal Son took on a real human body and soul. He did not merely appear human; he became fully human (John 1:14; Philippians 2:7; 1 John 4:2). He had to share our nature to save us.

That through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil. Key words. “Destroy” (katargēsē, render powerless, nullify, put out of action), as in 2 Timothy 1:10. Not annihilate, but disarm. “Power of death” (to kratos tou thanatou, the dominion of death). The devil holds the power of death in that he brought sin into the world, and sin brings death (Genesis 3; Romans 5:12; John 8:44). He accuses sinners and holds them under death’s penalty. By dying for sin, Christ removed the ground of the devil’s accusation and broke his grip (Colossians 2:14–15; Revelation 12:10–11). The irony: the devil’s weapon, death, became the means of his defeat.

And deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery. Key words. “Deliver” (apallaxē, set free, release). “Fear of death” (phobō thanatou). “Lifelong slavery” (dia pantos tou zēn enochoi ēsan douleias, liable to bondage all their lives). The fear of death is one of humanity’s deepest fears, shaping and enslaving all of life. Christ frees his people from it. For the believer, death is no longer a punishment but a passage to Christ (Philippians 1:21–23; 1 Corinthians 15:55–57).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the devil now has no activity at all; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8). It means his decisive power has been broken, and his final destruction is certain (Revelation 20:10). Nor does it mean believers never feel any fear of dying; it means that fear no longer rules them.

In a sentence. Since the children have flesh and blood, Jesus too shared in their humanity, so that by his death he might break the power of the one who holds the power of death, the devil, and set free all who have been held in slavery all their lives by their fear of death.

For worship. If you fear death, bring that fear to Christ. He has died and risen; death is defeated for those who are his.

verseByVerse.quote: For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.

For surely it is not angels that he helps. Key words. “Helps” (epilambanetai, takes hold of, lays hold of to help, grasps by the hand). The word pictures taking someone by the hand to rescue them (Matthew 14:31; Jeremiah 31:32, quoted in 8:9). Christ did not take hold of angels to save them. Fallen angels have no redeemer (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). He did not become an angel; he became a man.

But he helps the offspring of Abraham. Key words. “Offspring of Abraham” (spermatos Abraam, seed of Abraham). Abraham’s true children are all who share his faith, Jew and Gentile (Galatians 3:7, 29; Romans 4:16). Christ came to rescue them, as God promised Abraham (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). The readers, being Jewish, would hear this with special force.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ saves only ethnic Jews. Abraham’s offspring, in the New Testament sense, are all who believe (Romans 4:11–12). Nor does it mean Christ is indifferent to angels; the holy angels serve him gladly. But redemption is for human beings.

In a sentence. For it is clearly not angels that he takes hold of to help, but the descendants of Abraham.

For worship. Marvel that Christ took hold of human beings, not angels. He has taken hold of you, and he will not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.

Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect. Key words. “Had to” (ōpheilen, was obligated, needed). It was necessary, given the goal of saving human beings. “Like his brothers in every respect” (kata panta, in all things): body, soul, emotions, temptations, weakness, suffering, death. Everything human, except sin (4:15). He did not take a human body without a human mind, as some ancient heretics taught; he took full human nature.

So that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest. Key words. The first mention of the letter’s central theme: Jesus as high priest. “Merciful” (eleēmōn, compassionate): toward people, understanding their weakness. “Faithful” (pistos, trustworthy, reliable): toward God, carrying out his task perfectly. “High priest” (archiereus): the chief priest of Israel, who entered the Most Holy Place once a year to make atonement (Leviticus 16). Jesus is the true High Priest, to whom Aaron pointed.

In the service of God. Key words. Literally “in the things pertaining to God” (ta pros ton theon): the priest represents people before God.

To make propitiation for the sins of the people. Key words. “Make propitiation” (hilaskesthai, to propitiate, to turn away wrath by an offering, to atone). Propitiation means satisfying God’s just wrath against sin, so that he is favourable toward sinners. It includes expiation, the removal of sin itself. In the Old Testament, the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, was the place of propitiation (9:5), sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement. Christ is the propitiation for our sins (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2; 4:10). He bore the wrath we deserved (penal substitution). “The people” (tou laou): God’s people, the brothers of verses 11–17.

Where Christians differ: did Christ’s death turn away God’s wrath? Some modern theologians reject propitiation, arguing that God’s love does not need appeasing, and translate the word only as “expiation” (removal of sin). Verdict: Scripture teaches that God’s holy wrath is real (Romans 1:18; John 3:36), and that Christ’s death turned it away from his people by bearing it in their place (Isaiah 53:5–6, 10; Galatians 3:13). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son against his will; the Father in love sent the Son to be the propitiation (1 John 4:10). Propitiation and expiation go together: Christ removed our sin and satisfied God’s justice. This is penal substitutionary atonement, the heart of the gospel.

What it does not mean. “Made like his brothers in every respect” does not mean Jesus had a sinful nature or ever sinned. He was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (4:15). True humanity is not defined by sin; sin is a corruption of it.

In a sentence. That is why he had to be made like his brothers and sisters in every way, so that he could become a merciful and faithful high priest serving God, and make the atoning sacrifice that turns God’s wrath away from the sins of his people.

For worship. Thank Jesus, your merciful and faithful High Priest, who bore God’s wrath for your sins. There is no condemnation left for you.

verseByVerse.quote: For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.

For because he himself has suffered when tempted. Key words. “Suffered” (peponthen, perfect tense: suffered and still bears the experience). “Tempted” (peirastheis, tested, tried). Jesus was truly tempted: in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42–44), and throughout his life (Luke 22:28). His temptation involved suffering, because resisting temptation to the end is painful. He never gave in, so he felt the full force of temptation in a way no one who yields ever does.

He is able to help those who are being tempted. Key words. “Able” (dynatai, has the power). “Help” (boēthēsai, run to the aid of, come to the rescue when someone cries out). The word pictures running to answer a cry for help. Because he has been through it, he knows exactly what we face, and he has the power to help (4:15–16; 1 Corinthians 10:13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus could have sinned in the sense that his divine person could have been overcome. But his temptations were real, and his human nature felt their pull. Nor does it mean that he understands only in theory; he knows from experience.

In a sentence. Because he himself suffered when he was tested, he is able to come to the rescue of those who are being tested.

On a Tuesday. When you face temptation this week, cry out to Jesus. He has been there, and he will run to help you.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it.<sup>2</sup>For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,<sup>3</sup>how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard,<sup>4</sup>while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.<sup>5</sup>For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking.<sup>6</sup>It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him?<sup>7</sup>You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor,<sup>8</sup>putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.<sup>9</sup>But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.<sup>10</sup>For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.<sup>11</sup>For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers,<sup>12</sup>saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.”<sup>13</sup>And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”<sup>14</sup>Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil,<sup>15</sup>and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.<sup>16</sup>For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.<sup>17</sup>Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.<sup>18</sup>For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.

3.title: Greater Than Moses: Do Not Harden Your Hearts
3.overview:
Moses was the supreme figure in first-century Judaism: he built the tabernacle, received the law and spoke with God face to face. Hebrews honours him fully, “faithful in all God’s house”, then makes one decisive distinction: Moses was a servant in the house; Jesus is the Son over it.

The chapter then gives one of Scripture’s most searching warnings, from Psalm 95: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” The wilderness generation had everything and still fell in the desert through unbelief. The danger for the readers is the same: not dramatic denial but slow hardening. The remedy is practical: “exhort one another every day.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Jesus and Moses: Servant and Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer calls his readers, who share a heavenly calling, to fix their thoughts on Jesus, the one God sent and the high priest of the faith they confess. Jesus was faithful to God, just as Moses was faithful within God’s household. But Jesus deserves greater honour, as the builder of a house deserves more honour than the house itself, and God is the builder of everything. Moses served faithfully as a servant inside the house, pointing ahead to things that would be spoken later; Christ is faithful as the Son over the house. And we are that house, if we keep our confidence and our hope to the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
Servant and Son

Moses is not demoted but placed: faithful in God's house as a servant, while Christ is faithful over it as a son. The honour goes to the builder.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jesus is both apostle, sent from God, and high priest, going to God for us.

Now: The letter's standing prescription is to consider Jesus. Holding fast does not create the reality; it shows it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, holy brothers, you who share in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who was faithful to him who appointed him, just as Moses also was faithful in all God’s house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, holy brothers, you who share in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who was faithful to him who appointed him, just as Moses also was faithful in all God’s house.

Meaning first. Hebrews 3 shows that Jesus is greater than Moses and then gives the second warning, drawn from Israel’s failure in the wilderness. Moses was the most revered figure in Judaism, the mediator of the law, the one God spoke to face to face. The readers are urged to consider Jesus, who was faithful just as Moses was, but who deserves greater glory, as the builder of a house is greater than the house; Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, but Christ is faithful over it as the Son, and we are that house if we hold firm to the end (vv. 1–6). Then the warning (vv. 7–19), built on Psalm 95: the Holy Spirit still says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” as Israel did in the wilderness, when they tested God for forty years and he swore that they would not enter his rest. So the readers must watch that none of them has an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God; they must encourage one another daily, so that none is hardened by sin’s deceit, for we share in Christ only if we hold our confidence firm to the end. The wilderness generation saw God’s works, yet rebelled and died in the desert; they could not enter because of unbelief.

Therefore, holy brothers. Key words. “Therefore” (hothen, for this reason): because of all that Jesus is as the merciful high priest (2:17–18). “Holy” (hagioi, set apart): made holy by Christ (2:11). “Brothers”: Jesus calls them brothers (2:11), so does the author.

You who share in a heavenly calling. Key words. “Share” (metochoi, partners, partakers), as in 1:9. “Heavenly calling” (klēseōs epouraniou): a call from heaven, by God, and to heaven, to glory (Philippians 3:14). Not an earthly inheritance like Canaan, but a heavenly one (11:16).

Consider Jesus. Key words. “Consider” (katanoēsate, fix your mind on, think carefully about, observe closely). The cure for drifting is concentration on Jesus (12:2).

The apostle and high priest of our confession. Key words. “Apostle” (apostolon, sent one). The only place Jesus is called an apostle. He was sent by the Father to bring God’s word to us (John 17:3, 18). “High priest” (archierea): he represents us before God. As apostle, he comes from God to us; as high priest, he goes from us to God. Moses was in a sense both: God’s messenger and Israel’s intercessor; Aaron was the high priest. Jesus fulfils both roles. “Our confession” (homologias): the faith we publicly profess (4:14; 10:23).

Who was faithful to him who appointed him. Key words. “Faithful” (piston), as in 2:17. Jesus perfectly carried out the task the Father gave him (John 17:4).

Just as Moses also was faithful in all God’s house. Key words. From Numbers 12:7, where God defends Moses against Aaron and Miriam: Moses is faithful in all my house. “House” (oikos): God’s household, his people Israel. The author does not belittle Moses; he honours him. But he will show that Jesus is greater.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses was unfaithful or that the law was bad. Moses was faithful, and the law was God’s. Jesus fulfils what Moses began.

In a sentence. So, holy brothers and sisters, you who share in the call that comes from heaven, fix your thoughts on Jesus, the one God sent and the high priest of the faith we confess. He was faithful to the God who appointed him, just as Moses was faithful in all God’s household.

For worship. Consider Jesus today. Spend a few minutes doing nothing but thinking about who he is and what he has done.

parallels.desc: He is faithful in all my house

verseByVerse.quote: For Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses—as much more glory as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself. (For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses—as much more glory as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself. (For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God.)

For Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses. Key words. “Counted worthy” (ēxiōtai, deemed worthy, perfect tense: and remains so). “More glory” (pleionos doxēs). Moses’ face shone with reflected glory (Exodus 34:29–35; 2 Corinthians 3:7–18). Jesus is the radiance of God’s glory itself (1:3).

As much more glory as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself. Key words. “Builder” (kataskeuasas, the one who constructs, furnishes, establishes). Moses was part of the house, a member of God’s people, however prominent. Jesus is the builder of the house. The architect deserves more honour than the building.

For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God. Key words. God built everything. Since Jesus is the builder of God’s house, and God is the builder of all things, Jesus is identified with God. This connects with 1:2, 10: the Son created everything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses deserves no honour; he deserves great honour. It means Jesus deserves infinitely more, as the Creator deserves more than the creature.

In a sentence. Jesus has been judged worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has more honour than the house itself. Every house is built by someone, but the one who built everything is God.

For worship. Honour Jesus as the builder of the church and of all things. You are part of what he has built.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.

Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant. Key words. “Servant” (therapōn, attendant, honoured servant, a dignified word). Used of Moses in Numbers 12:7 (Greek). A servant of high honour, but still a servant within the house.

To testify to the things that were to be spoken later. Key words. “Testify” (martyrion, witness). Moses’ role was to bear witness to what God would say later, in the Son. The law, the tabernacle, the sacrifices and priesthood were all signs pointing forward to Christ (John 5:46; Luke 24:27).

But Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. Key words. “Over” (epi, set over, in charge of) rather than “in.” “As a son” (hōs huios). Servant versus Son; in the house versus over the house. The son is heir and master of the household (1:2). The title “Christ” (Messiah) appears for the first time in Hebrews.

And we are his house. Key words. “His house”: God’s house, over which Christ rules. The church is God’s household, his dwelling (1 Timothy 3:15; Ephesians 2:19–22; 1 Peter 2:5). Not a building but a people.
